topic.subject: chemistry
topic.title: Neutralisation, salts and carbonates
topic.scopeBasis: TGS 2025-26 Acids and Alkalis; TGS 2026-27 neutralisation and carbonates
topic.overview: Neutralisation reactions remove acidic and basic properties. Their product patterns make outcomes predictable and allow useful salts to be named.
learningGoals: Recall the precise Year 8 scientific vocabulary and symbols.
Apply the idea to an unfamiliar example rather than relying on recognition.
Use the command word, show working where needed and include every mark point.
mustMemoriseRules: acid + carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide
Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid forms sulfates and nitric acid forms nitrates.
A mixture reaches pH 7 only when suitable amounts react completely; adding excess reactant can leave it acidic or alkaline.
Carbonate reactions effervesce because carbon dioxide gas is produced.

mustMemoriseVocabulary.meaning: a reaction in which acid and base properties are removed to form salt and water
an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced in a reaction
a compound containing the carbonate group that reacts with acids to release carbon dioxide
visible fizzing caused by gas bubbles
a salt made from hydrochloric acid
a salt made from sulfuric acid
a salt made from nitric acid
more reactant than is needed to react completely with the other reactant

practicals.title: Investigate neutralisation
practicals.aim: Find how added alkali changes the pH of an acid.
practicals.variables: IV: volume of alkali added; DV: pH; controls: acid volume/concentrations/temperature/indicator amount.
practicals.method: Measure acid, add alkali in small measured portions, mix, record pH after each addition and use smaller additions near pH 7.
practicals.expectedResult: pH rises towards 7 and may exceed 7 if alkali becomes excess.
practicals.safety: Wear eye protection; use dilute solutions and a pipette filler, never mouth pipette.
practicals.evaluation: Use a pH probe for more objective values, smaller increments near the endpoint and repeats.

commonMistakes: Writing hydrogen instead of carbon dioxide for acid plus carbonate.
Naming the salt from the base rather than from both the metal and the acid.
examTips: First identify reaction pattern, then name the salt.
Salt first word comes from the metal/base; ending comes from the acid.
Do not assume every mixture of acid and alkali is exactly neutral.
beforeStartingPractice: Read the key rules once, cover them, then retrieve them aloud or in writing.
Use MC first for confidence, but finish with typed, calculation, practical or explanation evidence.
After an error, study the explanation; the same concept returns later in a different format and again after 2 and 7 days.

markPoints: Measure a fixed volume of acid.
Add alkali in measured small portions while mixing.
Monitor pH with indicator or preferably a calibrated pH probe.
Use smaller additions near pH 7.
Stop at about pH 7 rather than after a fixed guessed volume.
Repeat using the recorded volume for reliability.
Wear eye protection and use dilute solutions.

practicals.subject: chemistry
practicals.title: Investigate neutralisation
practicals.aim: Find how added alkali changes the pH of an acid.
practicals.variables: IV: volume of alkali added; DV: pH; controls: acid volume/concentrations/temperature/indicator amount.
practicals.method: Measure acid, add alkali in small measured portions, mix, record pH after each addition and use smaller additions near pH 7.
practicals.expectedResult: pH rises towards 7 and may exceed 7 if alkali becomes excess.
practicals.safety: Wear eye protection; use dilute solutions and a pipette filler, never mouth pipette.
practicals.evaluation: Use a pH probe for more objective values, smaller increments near the endpoint and repeats.
